note_tweet.text:
My husband’s family thinks I’m infertile. I let them spend $40,000 on fertility treatments for me while secretly taking birth control.

Before you call me evil, understand that my husband, Andrew, has always wanted children. He told me that before our first date, before he proposed, and before we got married.

I wanted him too. I just never wanted to be a mother.

I thought I could change my mind. Four years into our marriage, I still couldn’t imagine giving up my freedom, my body, or the life we’d built.

When we started trying for a baby, I panicked. Every negative test felt like a temporary escape. Then his mother suggested fertility testing, and I saw an opportunity I’m ashamed to admit I took.

I told Andrew we could try treatment.

I never told him I was still taking the pill.

I’ve been reading The Magic Mountain (pilled by @adam_tooze’s newsletter).

It feels like a fever dream, entering the mind of a young bourgeois engineer in pre-WWI Europe, where history is suspended and everything is slippery, symbolic, and feverish. 

I was thinking: “wow this is what a Freudian turn feels like from inside the European elite. And they have no idea what’s coming!”

It also reminds me of Lu Xun’s “In the Wine Shop” (在酒楼上) which is written around the same time, there’s a same feeling of historical suspension, of people caught in confusion when the old China was clashing with modernization.
